sections.body: Course design and teaching is the part of artificial intelligence work that helps instructors build and run courses, from mapping a curriculum to writing assessments, tutoring students, and turning notes into lecture materials. In practice, AI systems now draft learning outcomes, align topics to standards, generate quiz questions, score short answers, and produce feedback at a scale a single teacher cannot match. They also power course specific tutors that answer questions from assigned readings and create slide outlines or study guides from raw notes. The work is not just theoretical, because many of these functions appear in deployed products and in studies of classroom use. The focus is on augmenting teaching tasks, not replacing the instructor's judgement about what students need. The field draws on natural language processing, retrieval, and learning analytics to connect course content with student activity.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands unevenly. Curriculum mapping and learning outcome generation are fairly mature in narrow settings, because AI can match text to frameworks and suggest sequences, but it still misses context, local requirements, and the tacit knowledge of experienced teachers. Assessment generation is useful for draft items and rubrics, yet it struggles with validity, bias, and the difference between a plausible question and a fair one. Personalised learning and early warning systems can flag patterns in engagement or performance, but they often rely on limited data and can misread students who are quiet, disabled, or facing circumstances outside the course. Course specific tutors can answer from a closed set of materials, though they may hallucinate, miss nuance, or fail when a student asks a question that crosses topics. The honest limits are that none of these systems understand a classroom, a discipline, or a student the way a teacher does, and the site's 135 research papers show that evaluation remains hard, so the field has solved some drafting and retrieval tasks, not the deeper problems of motivation, equity, and learning.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: To navigate this section, start with Curriculum and Learning Outcomes for how AI helps map topics, skills, and standards into a coherent course plan. Generating Assessments covers the creation of quizzes, exams, rubrics, and feedback, and it is the page to read when the question is how to produce or judge assessment items. Personalised Learning and Early Warning looks at adaptive paths and risk signals, and it is where the ethical and data limits of student monitoring come into view. Course-Specific AI Tutors explains how a tutor can be grounded in a single syllabus or reading list, and it is the place to go for retrieval, grounding, and dialogue design. Lecture Materials from Notes shows how raw notes, transcripts, or outlines can become slides, handouts, or study aids. Together these pages move from planning, to assessment, to personalisation, to tutoring, to materials, which is the full teaching cycle this section describes.
